title: Why Convolutional Networks? 🖼️
description: Understand why fully‑connected layers fail on images and how convolutions exploit spatial structure.

slides.title: The Problem with Fully‑Connected Layers 🚫
slides.content:
# Images are Not Flat

A 224×224 RGB image has **150,528** input values. A single fully‑connected hidden layer of 1000 neurons would need **150 million** parameters – just for the first layer!

* Too many parameters → overfitting.
* Ignores spatial structure: nearby pixels are related, far apart are not.
* Small shifts break the model.

quizData.question: Why do fully‑connected layers struggle with large images?

options.text: They can't handle 2D data at all
The number of parameters explodes and spatial relationships are lost
They are too slow on GPU

quizData.explanation: FC layers flatten input, losing spatial context and requiring enormous weight matrices.

slides.title: How Our Eyes Work 👁️
slides.content:
## Receptive Fields

Visual neurons respond to a small region of the retina, not the whole image. Similarly, a **convolutional layer** applies small filters (kernels) that look at local patches, and slides over the image.

This gives:
* **Parameter sharing** – same filter used everywhere.
* **Locality** – a filter only connects to a small region.
* **Translation invariance** (with pooling).

slides.title: Imagine a 3×3 Filter
slides.content: Visualising a simple edge detector kernel.
slides.codeSnippet:
import torch

# A 3x3 Sobel-like kernel for vertical edges
kernel = torch.tensor([[-1, 0, 1],
                       [-2, 0, 2],
                       [-1, 0, 1]], dtype=torch.float32)
print(kernel)
# This kernel, when convolved over an image, highlights vertical lines.

slides.title: CNNs Preserve Spatial Hierarchy 🌳
slides.content:
## From Edges to Objects

Early layers detect edges and textures. Deeper layers combine them into shapes, then object parts, then whole objects – all while keeping spatial arrangement.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## The Power of Weight Sharing

A convolutional layer with 32 filters of size 3×3 on 3‑channel input has only 32×3×3×3 + 32 = 896 parameters – tiny compared to millions!
